author: Our World in Data
body:
Global electricity generation has tripled since 1985 — most of this growth came from Asia.

In 1985, the world generated around 10,000 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity. In 2024, it produced just over 30,000 TWh — three times as much.

Three-quarters of this increase came from Asia. The chart shows how generation has grown, both globally and in each region.

Yes, population growth explains some of this. But two other drivers were even stronger: more people gained access to electricity, and they consumed more of it. In the early 1990s, fewer than half of South Asians had access to basic electricity. Today, access is almost universal.

At the same time, electricity generation per person increased by almost 450% — far faster than in any other region. Outside of Asia, it has barely changed. This is why, globally, per-person consumption has only doubled.

This growth has given households more and better energy services, and it has also powered a huge expansion of industry.

(written by Hannah Ritchie)

Explore how electricity generation and sources have changed across the world: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/electricity-mix

The bottom 20% lost 6%, falling to $14,400.

author: Our World in Data
body:
📝 New article on Our World in Data: No matter how you ask, more Americans are negative than positive about AI.

Online, the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence are intensely debated. But the online world is far from representative, and what people report in a survey can shift quite substantially when a question is worded slightly differently or when respondents can choose their answer from different options. So instead of relying on just one survey, this article puts together five recent high-quality surveys of adults in the United States.

The survey’s wording does matter. When a middle answer is offered, many people take it — 37% did in Pew’s recent survey — and a smaller share reports a positive view: in both Pew’s and Gallup’s surveys, only 9% chose it.

Yet the overall result is consistent: every survey finds that more Americans have a negative view of AI than a positive one. In Pew’s survey, 52% say they are “more concerned than excited”, and 9% are “more excited than concerned” — a ratio of more than five to one.

When people have strong feelings, they are mostly negative. In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an “extremely bad” thing for society, and just 2% said “extremely good”. People’s worries extend to the most extreme risks: in a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% of Americans said they are somewhat concerned and 38% said they are very concerned that future AI systems could potentially threaten human survival.

Concern about AI is not confined to one party: in Pew’s survey, 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are more concerned than excited about AI. There is no question that many find the prospects of AI exciting. But what these surveys show is that for more Americans, the concerns are larger.

Read the article by Max Roser: https://ourworldindata.org/no-matter-how-you-ask-more-americans-are-negative-than-positive-about-ai

author: Aziz Sunderji
body:
How are Americans doing, financially speaking? 

My new map story, Pulling Apart, starts with that question. To go by national statistics, Americans are doing just fine: unemployment is low and stock market wealth is booming. But these figures hide how many households are struggling. Wages at the bottom have barely grown, and the poorer half of American households holds just 2% of the nation’s wealth.

It’s the same in housing. National prices have been rising slowly and steadily. But there is no single national housing market. There are, in effect, two worlds within it. In richer, whiter neighborhoods with low crime and good schools, prices are rising and homes are selling. In neighborhoods that are mostly Black and Hispanic, with more modest homes, more crime and weaker schools, prices are falling and far fewer homes sell.

The story maps those two worlds pulling apart across five cities: Philadelphia, Detroit, Phoenix, Atlanta and Indianapolis. Every map in the story was made with ProMap, which you can use to explore the same data for any neighborhood in the country.

Read Pulling Apart: https://homeeconomics.us/promap?story=r3c5q7
